Seems obvious, but for those who are not familiar with figma API, use a PAT (Personnal Access Token) to generate client id  / secret :

> curl -X POST https://api.figma.com/v1/oauth/mcp/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Figma-Token: $FIGMA_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "client_name": "Claude Code (figma)",
    "redirect_uris": ["http://127.0.0.1:19876/mcp/oauth/callback"],
    "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
    "response_types": ["code"],
    "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
  }'

To get your PAT $FIGMA_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN see https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/authentication/#use-the-personal-access-token

**TL;DR;** Figma >Settings > Security > Personal access tokens, then Generate new token

Note: if you are on a server or virtual machine with no access to 127.0.0.1, and no time / option to expose the temp auth server, just curl the last redirect:

> curl http://127.0.0.1:19876/mcp/oauth/callback?code=xxx&state=xxx

I spent some time with Claude and it finds the problem in how tree-sitter loads. Check below.

---

MarkdownRenderable (tree-sitter) broken in Bun compiled binaries — Worker entry point not bundled.

`MarkdownRenderable` (and any tree-sitter-based syntax highlighting) renders as plain text when the application is distributed as a Bun compiled binary (`bun build --compile`). It works correctly in dev mode (`bun run dev`) and appears to work when running the compiled binary from the build directory, but breaks when the binary is installed to a different location (e.g., via Homebrew).

## Root Cause

`TreeSitterClient.startWorker()` spawns a Web Worker using:

```ts
worker_path = new URL("./parser.worker.js", import.meta.url).href;
if (!existsSync(resolve(import.meta.dirname, "parser.worker.js"))) {
    worker_path = new URL("./parser.worker.ts", import.meta.url).href;
}
this.worker = new Worker(worker_path);
```

**`bun build --compile` does not automatically bundle Web Worker entry points into the compiled binary.** The `parser.worker.js` file is not embedded in the output executable.

When the compiled binary runs:

1. `import.meta.dirname` resolves to the binary's directory (e.g., `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/huba/0.0.15/bin/`)
2. `existsSync` check for `parser.worker.js` next to the binary → fails (only the binary is installed)
3. Falls back to `parser.worker.ts` URL → also doesn't exist
4. `new Worker(url)` fails with: `BuildMessage: ModuleNotFound resolving "/$bunfs/root/parser.worker.ts" (entry point)`
5. The worker error is caught, `TreeSitterClient` never initializes
6. `MarkdownRenderable` receives no highlights → renders as plain unformatted text

## Why It Appears to Work Locally

- **`bun run dev`**: Runs from source. `parser.worker.js` exists in `node_modules/@opentui/core/` and is resolved normally.
- **Compiled binary in build directory**: The `/$bunfs/root/` virtual filesystem paths may still resolve on the same machine where compilation happened, or there's a cached tree-sitter state in `~/.local/share/opentui/` from previous dev runs.

## Reproduction

Minimal reproduction of the Bun limitation:

```ts
// main.ts
const worker = new Worker(new URL("./worker.ts", import.meta.url).href);
worker.onmessage = (e) => console.log("OK:", e.data);
worker.onerror = (e) => console.error("FAIL:", e.message);
```

```ts
// worker.ts
declare var self: { postMessage: (data: any) => void };
self.postMessage("hello");
```

```bash
bun build --compile main.ts --outfile ./test-binary
./test-binary          # may work (same location)
cp ./test-binary /tmp/
/tmp/test-binary       # FAIL: ModuleNotFound resolving "/$bunfs/root/worker.ts"
```

## Impact

Any application using `@opentui/core`'s `MarkdownRenderable`, `CodeRenderable`, or `DiffRenderable` (anything relying on `TreeSitterClient`) will silently lose syntax highlighting when distributed as a compiled Bun binary.

The failure is silent — no visible error to the user, just plain text output instead of highlighted markdown/code.

## Environment

- Bun: 1.3.2
- Platform: macOS (darwin-arm64), also affects Linux
- Distribution method: Homebrew (standalone binary)

## Suggested Solutions

1. **Inline the worker code** — Use `new Worker(new Blob([workerSource]))` or Bun's inline worker support to avoid the need for a separate file entry point.

2. **Main-thread fallback** — Detect the compiled binary environment (e.g., `import.meta.url` contains `/$bunfs/`) and fall back to running tree-sitter parsing on the main thread when Worker creation fails.

3. **Graceful degradation with clear warning** — If the worker fails to spawn, log a visible warning and fall back to unhighlighted rendering, so consumers know what's happening rather than silentl

We independently arrived at the same fix (parentID matching instead of ID ordering) and adopted this approach in our fork. The `shouldExitLoop` extraction is clean and well-tested — we also extracted a `shouldWrapSystemReminder` helper for the system-reminder wrapping site, following the same pattern. Both run without issues on our end and cleanly resolve the infinite loop when client/server clocks diverge. +1 for merge.

We adopted this PR's `sortMessages`/`selectAssistants`/`splitMessages` utilities in our fork. The `time.created`-first ordering + role rank tiebreaker approach works well for frontend rendering. One note for the maintainers: we also found that `time_created` in the backend DB is client-provided for user messages (set from `msg.time.created` in `updateMessage`), so the same ordering approach isn't safe for backend chronological comparisons — we used index-based position instead for backend fixes to fork/revert/prompt-wrapping.

We've been investigating the same root cause and took a tactical approach (fixing consumers to use array position instead of ID ordering for fork/revert/prompt-wrapping). While that eliminates the symptoms, this PR's approach of making the server authoritative for message IDs eliminates the bug class entirely. The `clientMessageID` field for optimistic reconciliation is the right pattern. Would love to see this merged — it's the complete solution.

Hey @RicardoMonteiroSimoes, sorry, missed this! This PR implements tier-based model selection, not fallback chains. Here's the distinction:

**What this PR does:**

- Define 3 tiers (`quick`, `standard`, `advanced`) mapped to specific models in config
- Agents use `model_tier` parameter to select appropriate capability/cost level
- Agent-level tiers override global tiers for customization

```json
"model_tiers": {
  "quick": { "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5" },
  "standard": { "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5" },
  "advanced": { "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-4-5" }
}
```

**What you're describing (fallback chains):**

```json
"models": ["opus", "sonnet", "gpt-5.3"]
```

This would try models in order if earlier ones fail/unavailable.

**Why tiers vs fallback chains:**

Tiers solve a different problem - cost optimization through capability matching. A file search uses `quick` (Haiku), architecture review uses `advanced` (Opus). Same agent, different task complexity = different model.

Your fallback chain idea is valuable for provider redundancy! It's just out of scope for this PR.

@jamessimas unfortunately, they confirmed that while Fine-Grained PATs are conditionally supported for official tools like the Copilot CLI, this authentication method is not currently supported for third-party tools like OpenCode. They also explicitly warned that spoofing the `Copilot-Integration-Id` header to get around this could result in accounts being flagged for abuse.

They declined to provide a temporary exception and have instead logged this as formal product feedback for their leadership team to review. At this time, there is no timeline or guarantee on when or if this will be officially supported.

My personal takeaway is that restricting PAT authentication specifically is a strategic decision rather than just missing code. While they allow OpenCode for standard interactive use, locking down PATs ensures that automated, headless workflows remain strictly exclusive to GitHub's official tools.

GNAP is interesting, but a limited system focused on coding that breaks down under the demands of knowledge-work or general task performance. It isn't a true substitute - too many failure points alongside significant constraints.

I think a multi-caller tasking system with a shared state system is going to outperform systems focused on coordinating coding projects. Such systems adaptively specialize for the work they perform, as they have the capacity to learn, and then recursively build whatever is required to optimize the workflow and domain that the user is focused upon. 

I think what people need to focus on is not the implementation part of coding workflows - it's the cognitively demanding systems design and spec development.
